teaching.text: The **vocal folds** form a vibrating membrane. **Mode 1–5** name patterns of movement across that whole membrane.
children: The small pairs, such as **(2, 1)**, count moving regions along the membrane’s two directions, rather than identifying separate masses.
In **mode 1**, the membrane moves together. In **mode 2**, one region moves up while another moves down. Higher modes divide the surface into more regions moving against one another.
Several modes can occur at once, and their movements add together in **All 5 modes**. The marked **pickup point** identifies where that combined movement is measured.

teaching.text: A **spectrum** separates the combined movement into its frequency contributions. The illustrated source has **harmonics**, whole-number multiples of its lowest frequency, **F0**, the fundamental frequency.
children: The spectrum’s horizontal axis is **Frequency (Hz)**, with hertz meaning cycles per second. Its vertical axis is **relative amplitude**, the strength of each measured contribution. Equal spike heights mean equal measured strengths, rather than equal frequencies.

The assigned **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** illustrate the whole-number spacing. These are teaching frequencies for this membrane illustration, not a rule that every membrane has that natural frequency series.

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** has one end held still and one free to move. Here **fixed bottom** and **free top** locate those ends; every allowed mode must fit both conditions.
children: The fixed end is a **node**, with no displacement during the cycle. The free end is an **antinode**, where movement is largest.
**Mode 1–4** count the allowed whole-string patterns.

teaching.text: These end conditions allow the **odd harmonics**, at one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency. The second allowed mode is therefore three times the lowest frequency, rather than twice it.
children: The example frequencies **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz** show this odd-multiple spacing directly. In the spectrum, horizontal position gives frequency and spike height gives amplitude; equal heights indicate equally strong measured contributions.

teaching.text: For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end lowers the first mode to half the frequency of the fixed–fixed system.
A **quarter-wave packet** runs from a node to an antinode. One packet fits the first mode of a fixed–free system because the pattern starts still and ends moving.
children: **Mode numbers** count allowed vibration patterns. **Quarter-wave counts** describe pieces of those patterns within the string’s length.

teaching.text: Mode 2 fits **three packets** in the same length. Modes 3 and 4 fit five and seven. More packets mean a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency.
children: **3 × 100 Hz** means that mode 2 vibrates three times as fast as the illustrated 100 Hz first mode. The factor describes relative frequency, not three strings or three separate masses.
An even number of packets would finish at a node. That would violate the moving condition at the free end, so the allowed counts are odd.
The packets describe parts of one standing pattern, rather than separate objects traveling along the system.

teaching.text: The **air in the vocal tract** is a second vibrating system, separate from the vocal folds. Its movement is **longitudinal**, back and forth along the length of the tract.

In the neutral-tube model, the left **fixed** end represents the closed vocal-fold end, and the right **free** end represents the open lips. Air next to the closed end cannot move back and forth there; air at the lips can.
children: The blue circles are model masses representing portions of moving air. The connecting springs represent the air’s restoring response as it compresses and expands.

teaching.text: The air’s resonant frequencies are **formants**. **F1** is the first resonance and **F2** is the second. For a uniform fixed–free tube, their frequencies follow the odd-multiple pattern.
children: The upper **Mode 1, F1-like** row and lower **Mode 2, F2-like** row show two possible patterns of the same air column. The **3× faster** label compares their repetition rates in this uniform model.
The **1/3** and **2/3** marks give positions measured from the closed end. They locate the /a/ and /i/ constriction regions; the /u/ mark is at the open lip end.

teaching.text: Air can **move back and forth** while neighboring portions stay nearly the same distance apart. That is strong movement with little compression.
children: The blue circles represent portions of air. **Schwa** names the neutral vowel model. **Mod1@F1**, **Mod2@F2** and **Mod3@F3** mean mode 1 at its first formant, mode 2 at its second formant, and mode 3 at its third formant.

teaching.text: Air can also **compress and expand** as neighboring portions approach and separate. This changing spacing supplies the restoring effect called **springiness**.
children: Near the closed end, the air has little movement but strong compression and expansion. At the open end, the air moves strongly with little compression.

teaching.text: In **mode 1**, motion becomes stronger toward the open end while springiness becomes weaker. Higher modes alternate between regions of strong motion and regions of strong compression more times along the tract.

At each marked position, ask whether the air mainly **travels together** or **compresses and expands**. The answer comes from the movement throughout the cycle, rather than the air’s position in one still frame.
children: **A–F label marked positions**, so they identify places to compare within the air pattern. The mode labels identify which pattern is being considered; a lettered position is not a separate mode.
**Mod1@F1**, **Mod2@F2** and **Mod3@F3** pair each mode with its formant frequency.
A region where the slices approach and separate strongly is springy. A region where they travel together with little change in spacing mainly shows the moving mass.

teaching.text: A **constriction** increases both the effective mass and the stiffness of the air. Its effect depends on the mode’s behavior at that location.
children: Where compression is strong and movement is small, the stiffness increase matters more, so the formant rises.
Where movement is strong and compression is small, the mass increase matters more, so the formant falls.

teaching.text: A **constriction** is a narrowing of the vocal tract. The MRI images show that different vowels place this narrowing in different locations.
children: **High/low** and **front/back** describe the tongue’s position. **Central** places the neutral vowel between those extremes. The **glottis** is the opening between the vocal folds, used as the starting point for the distance marks.
For **/i/** in dean, the tongue is high and forward, narrowing the tract near two thirds of the distance from the glottis.
For **/u/** in dune, the model emphasizes the narrowing at the lips. For **/a/** in Don, it emphasizes a narrowing farther back, near one third of the distance from the glottis.
The central vowel in done is the neutral comparison, with no marked constriction in this model. Dan has a low, front tongue position.

teaching.text: The location matters because **each air mode has its own pattern of motion and compression**. The same narrowing can therefore affect F1 and F2 differently.
Compare **mode 1 and mode 2 at the same location**. Each is a pattern for the whole air column, and each uses that location differently.
children: The upper row is **mode 1**, associated with **F1**; the lower row is **mode 2**, associated with **F2**. **1/3** and **2/3** mark positions along the tract from the fixed end, not frequency ratios.
At the lips, both modes have strong air movement. Inside the tract, one mode can have strong movement where the other has strong compression.
A constriction changes F1 according to mode 1’s behavior there, and changes F2 according to mode 2’s behavior there. F1 and F2 are resonances of the air, separate from the vocal-fold harmonics.

teaching.text: For **/u/**, narrowing at the lips **loads the free end**. Loading means adding effective mass at the part of the air column that moves strongly.
children: The red-highlighted region identifies the constriction change, and the blue circles represent the portions of air whose movement is being followed.

teaching.text: Both mode 1 and mode 2 have strong movement at the lips, with little compression. The increased mass therefore has the larger effect in both modes, giving **F1 ↓ and F2 ↓**.
children: The **↓** arrows mean lower formant frequencies, rather than downward movement of air.
The constriction also increases stiffness, but that increase matters little where compression is small.
The low formants in vowels such as dune are consistent with this prediction.

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is near **two thirds (2/3) of the distance from the closed end**. The air behaves differently there in the first two modes.
children: The red-highlighted region identifies the constriction change, and the blue circles represent the portions of air whose movement is being followed.
In **mode 1**, the air mainly moves back and forth. The increase in effective mass dominates, so **F1 falls**.
In **mode 2**, the air mainly compresses and expands. The increase in stiffness dominates, so **F2 rises**.

teaching.text: The result is **F1 ↓ and F2 ↑**, low F1 and high F2. A transition from the neutral vowel into /i/ therefore lowers the first formant and raises the second.
children: The arrows describe **changes in formant frequency**, rather than the direction in which the air travels.

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is farther back, near **one third (1/3) of the distance from the closed end**.
children: The red-highlighted region identifies the constriction change, and the blue circles represent the portions of air whose movement is being followed.
In **mode 1**, strong compression makes the increase in stiffness matter more, so **F1 rises**.
In **mode 2**, strong movement makes the increase in effective mass matter more, so **F2 falls**.

teaching.text: The result, **F1 ↑ and F2 ↓**, brings the first two formants closer together. It reverses the /i/ pattern because the constriction acts at a different place in each mode.
children: The arrows mean a **higher F1 frequency and a lower F2 frequency**, rather than directions of air movement.

teaching.text: **Motion** describes how far a portion of air moves back and forth. **Compression** describes how much the distance between neighboring portions changes.
children: The blue circles represent portions of air. **Schwa** names the neutral vowel model. **Mod1@F1**, **Mod2@F2** and **Mod3@F3** mean mode 1 at its first formant, mode 2 at its second formant, and mode 3 at its third formant.
Neighboring portions can move far together and remain evenly spaced. Elsewhere, their individual movement can be small while the distance between them changes strongly.

teaching.text: The first three modes alternate between these behaviors at different places. To predict a constriction’s effect, follow the relevant mode and check **movement and changing spacing at the constriction**.
The **vocal-fold source** supplies harmonics. **F0**, its lowest frequency, also sets the spacing between those harmonics.
children: The three source rows use **F0 = 100, 250 and 350 Hz**. Each row covers the same **0–4,000 Hz** horizontal range, so the spacing of its stems can be compared directly.
Each vertical stem is one **source harmonic**. Its horizontal position gives its frequency; the number of stems in this shared range changes because the harmonic spacing changes.
A low F0 puts the harmonics close together. A high F0 places them farther apart.
Greater vocal-fold mass and lower stiffness favor a lower F0. Lower mass and greater stiffness favor a higher F0.

teaching.text: Changes in **F0 over time** contribute to intonation. The same words, “the dog slept here,” can sound like a statement or a question when their pitch pattern changes.
The **vocal tract is the filter**. Its resonances, the **formants**, make source harmonics near those frequencies stronger and harmonics farther away weaker.
children: The vertical marks locate the **formants along a frequency axis**. **1k** means **1,000 Hz**, so the horizontal position, rather than the height of a mark, shows how high a formant is.

teaching.text: For the neutral uniform tube, the formants follow the odd-multiple pattern. Constrictions change that pattern.
children: **Schwa /ə/** is the neutral comparison. Its illustrated **500 and 1,500 Hz** marks locate F1 and F2. The vowel rows change those resonance positions; the numbers are example formant frequencies, not source-harmonic numbers.
**/u/** has low F1 and low F2. **/i/** has low F1 and high F2. **/a/** has a higher F1 and a lower F2 than the neutral comparison.

teaching.text: The source supplies the harmonic frequencies, while the filter shapes **their relative strengths**. The resulting spectrum contains both influences.
The **same vowel filter** can produce different-looking spectra when **F0** changes. F0 determines how many source harmonics fall near the formants.
children: Read **down one vowel column** to keep the filter fixed while changing the source from **F0 100** to **250** to **350 Hz**. Read **across one row** to keep F0 fixed while changing the vowel filter.

The **dashed red ticks** locate the formant targets, the **gray curves** trace the filter shape, and the **colored stems** show the actual harmonics after filtering. Stem position gives frequency; stem height gives amplitude.
With a low F0, many closely spaced harmonics show the rises and falls of the filter clearly.
With a high F0, the widely spaced harmonics can leave few or no harmonics near a formant. The vowel pattern then becomes harder to identify from the spectrum.

teaching.text: A spectral slice can be used to identify the source harmonics and measure F0. The lowest harmonic gives the fundamental, and the others occur at its multiples.
A **spectrum** shows frequency and amplitude at one moment. A **spectrogram** shows how that information changes over time.
children: The small spectra put **frequency across** and **amplitude upward**. In the large spectrogram, that frequency axis runs **upward**, and the left-to-right axis is **time**.
The amplitude key maps **high amplitude to black**, medium amplitude to gray and low amplitude to white. A taller spectral peak therefore becomes a darker mark at its frequency and moment.

teaching.text: The dark formant bands trace the changing vocal tract. During **/ia/**, **F1 rises and F2 falls** as the sound changes from /i/ toward /a/.

A **neural network** can use **F1 and F2**, the frequencies of the first two air resonances, to recognize a vowel. These two input measurements, in **hertz**, describe one recording; the output predicts its vowel identity.
children: **Weights**, often written W, are the numbers that control how the network uses its inputs. Training changes these weights so that the network’s decisions better match the known vowels.

teaching.text: A **fully connected network** connects every neuron in one layer to every neuron in the next. Its hidden layers process the values between the input and output.
children: **Input · 2** counts the two input neurons, one for F1 and one for F2. **Hidden 1 · 3** means the first hidden layer has three neurons; the next hidden layers have two and four.
**Output · 5** counts five vowel alternatives for the same recording. Those outputs represent the vowels in done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.

teaching.text: Each hidden neuron takes an **inner product**, also called a **weighted sum**. It multiplies each incoming value by its connection weight, then adds the products.
children: This is a **linear network**, with no activation function between layers. Each layer’s results become the next layer’s inputs.

teaching.text: The **circles are neurons**, and the small numbers on their connections are **weights**, controlling how incoming values contribute to the next neuron. The **320 and 2,000** at the left are the input formants in hertz, one F1–F2 pair.
children: The connection label **−0.35** is a negative weight, while **0.30** is positive. For a positive incoming value, the first subtracts from the weighted sum and the second adds to it.
A weight’s **magnitude**, its size apart from the sign, sets how strongly the incoming value contributes.

teaching.text: Before training, the weights are **random**, so they do not yet contain useful knowledge about the vowels. A low F1 and high F2 identify an /i/-like input, but random weights can still lead to the wrong answer.
In **forward propagation**, the formants pass through the network one layer at a time. Each neuron calculates a weighted sum, and those values become the inputs to the next layer.
children: The **320 and 2,000** input values are F1 and F2 in hertz. The labels under the layers count neurons, while the numbers along the lines are connection weights.

teaching.text: The final scores are converted into a **probability distribution** over the five vowels. The probabilities add up to one, and the largest identifies the network’s choice.
children: **p(word)** means the probability assigned to each word’s vowel. The **0.5** bar for done means 50% of the illustrated probability, while **0.1** means 10%. A longer bar means a more likely answer, not a higher formant frequency.
Here the network favors done even though the input is /i/, as in dean. A valid probability distribution can still give the wrong answer.

teaching.text: A **target** supplies the known vowel. Training uses the difference between the prediction and the target to change the weights, so a repeated presentation of those formants can favor dean more strongly.
**PyTorch** provides tools for building a neural network in Python. **nn.Sequential** puts the processing layers in the order that the inputs pass through them.
children: **torch** names the library, **nn** is the short name used for its neural-network tools, and **net** is the variable holding this network.

teaching.text: Each **nn.Linear** specifies the number of inputs and outputs for a weighted-sum layer.
children: In **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, two values enter and three neuron values come out. The full **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** sequence counts the successive layer widths, carrying F1 and F2 through the hidden layers to five vowel scores.
The final **nn.Linear(4, 5)** receives four hidden activations and produces those five scores. Each layer’s output size matches the next layer’s input size.
Setting **bias=False** removes the **bias**, an extra constant that would otherwise be added to a weighted sum.

teaching.text: Declaring this structure **does not train it**. Training also requires examples, their correct answers, and instructions for adjusting the weights.
A **neural network** processes numbers to make a decision. Here its two inputs are **F1 and F2**, the first two vocal-tract resonances, measured in **Hz**, or cycles per second.
children: The input neurons receive the two measurements from one recording. **Hidden layers** process them between the input and output. The five output neurons represent the vowels in done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.

teaching.text: The network is **fully connected**, so every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer. Each connection has a **weight**, a number that controls its contribution.
children: The signed numbers on the connections are weights. The sequence **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** counts neurons in successive layers; an **activation** is a neuron’s current numerical response.
The weights hold the network’s learned knowledge. Their signs and sizes determine how the incoming values combine in a weighted sum.

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the layers to produce an answer. Each neuron calculates an **inner product**, multiplying incoming values by their weights and adding the products.
children: The example supplies **F1 = 320 Hz** and **F2 = 2,000 Hz**. In **w₁F1 + w₂F2**, **w₁** and **w₂** name the two connection weights into the top hidden neuron.
A number **inside a hidden circle** is its activation. A number **on a connecting line** is a weight. **−0.4 appears in both places** here, so its position determines which role it has.
For that neuron, the F1 contribution is positive and the F2 contribution is negative. Their combined effect gives the negative activation passed to the next layer.

teaching.text: One layer’s activations become the next layer’s inputs. The same weighted-sum operation continues until the output layer has a score for each vowel.
**Softmax** converts the final **scores**, or **logits zᵢ**, into **probabilities pᵢ** over the five vowels. The probabilities total one, and a larger score gives a larger probability.
children: The index **i** identifies a vowel alternative, and **Σ** in the softmax expression means to add across those alternatives.
**55.7% for done** is the highest probability, so done is the network’s choice. The percentage reports confidence in a vowel category, rather than a frequency in hertz.
Making a decision with learned weights is called **inference**.

teaching.text: The **Computed Output** percentages give the current prediction. The **Desired Output**, or **target**, specifies the vowel that actually produced the formants.
children: A **one-hot target** has a one for the correct vowel and zeros for the others. Here the one beside **dean** identifies the answer for this recording.

teaching.text: The **error**, measured by the **loss**, is the mismatch between prediction and target. The example favors done when the target is dean, so learning should increase the support for dean and reduce the support for the wrong answers.

**Backpropagation** works from the output toward the input to calculate how the error depends on the weights. **Stochastic gradient descent**, or **SGD**, uses that information to make small changes in the weights.
children: In the weight-update expression, **W** is a weight, **L** is the loss, and **η** is the learning rate. The **gradient**, written **∂L/∂W**, describes how changing that weight affects the loss. The left arrow means to replace the current weight with its adjusted value.

The connection numbers show weights being adjusted. The values inside the circles are saved **forward-pass activations**, reused for the backward calculation. A new forward pass recalculates them using the changed weights, which can improve the prediction.

teaching.text: The **circled +0.1 weight** multiplies the positive **1.57 activation** feeding done. Increasing that weight increases its contribution to done’s output score and probability.
children: Because the correct answer is dean, making done more likely increases the error. **Decreasing this marked weight** moves its contribution in the useful direction.

teaching.text: The **circled +0.005** is an early connection weight from F1. Changing it changes a hidden activation, then later activations, before the output probabilities change.
children: Its small numerical size does not reveal the useful adjustment direction. Its effect passes through later positive and negative weights, so the backward calculation must account for the whole path to the error.

teaching.text: **Backpropagation starts at the output** because the last weights have the most direct connection to the error. The output probabilities depend on those weights immediately.
children: **W2** names the first set of processing weights, and **W5** names the last set. The subscripts identify their positions in this network; each set contains many individual connection weights.

teaching.text: The effect of an early weight is more involved. Changing it affects several later layers, so its contribution to the error **includes the effects of the later weights**.
children: Working backward makes the error information from those later calculations available when the earlier weights are considered.

teaching.text: This is **dynamic programming**: solve the smaller dependent problems and reuse their results to solve the larger ones. **SGD** supplies the small weight adjustments; dynamic programming explains the backward order of the calculation.
Training pairs each recording with its known answer in two **matrices**, or tables of numbers.
children: **Formant_Inputs, 110 × 2** means 110 recording rows with the two columns **F1 and F2**. **TrueVowel_Outputs, 110 × 5** means matching rows with five vowel-answer columns.

In the highlighted row, **320 and 2,000 Hz** are the formants for one dean recording. Its **one-hot target** has one in the dean column and zeros in the other columns, so the five entries describe one answer.

teaching.text: The rows must **stay matched across the tables**. A pair of formants from dean must be paired with the dean target.
children: Training compares the computed output with this fixed target and changes the weights. Reordering only one table would pair recordings with the wrong answers.

teaching.text: The PyTorch **import** commands provide the neural-network tools.
children: **X** holds the formant-input table and **Y** holds the target table. Their shown sizes, **110 × 2** and **110 × 5**, count recording rows and measurement or answer columns. **torch.load** reads the saved tables, and **float** puts their entries in a numerical format that supports decimal values.

teaching.text: **nn.Sequential** describes the order of the layers. **nn.Linear** describes a layer that combines incoming numbers through weighted sums.
children: **net** is the network variable. **net(X)** means process the input table X through that network. In **Linear(2, 3)**, two values enter and three neuron values come out.
The processing sizes are **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**. Four Linear instructions process the input through three hidden layers and into five output scores.
The two input neurons only receive F1 and F2. They do not require a separate Linear instruction.

teaching.text: The learning commands compare the prediction with the target and adjust the weights.
children: The update procedure **sgd** receives the trainable weights from **net.parameters()**. **lr = 0.1** sets the learning rate, controlling the size of each adjustment.

**zero_grad()** clears the previous stored weight-change information. The **CrossEntropyLoss** call compares **net(X)**, the computed scores, with **Y**, the known answers, and **loss** stores the mismatch.
**loss.backward()** calculates how that loss depends on the weights. **sgd.step()** applies the weight adjustment.

teaching.text: This program takes **one training step using all rows together**. Declaring a network, calculating its loss, and updating its weights are distinct operations.
An **activation function** changes a neuron’s weighted sum into the value passed on. The S-shaped **sigmoid**, written **σ**, transforms the weighted sum **z** into a response between zero and one.
children: The horizontal **Linear Activation** axis plots z, and the vertical **Sigmoid Activation** axis plots σ(z). Each plotted pair gives the input weighted sum and its resulting response.

teaching.text: A large negative sum produces a response near zero; a large positive sum produces one near one. The marked points show **σ(−4) ≈ 0.018** and **σ(4) ≈ 0.982**.
children: Near the middle of the curve, a small input change can make a substantial output change. At the flatter ends, even a larger input change has little effect.

teaching.text: The biological motivation is the near **on-or-off** behavior associated with neurons and Adrian’s work. Sigmoid gives an artificial neuron a bounded response, while still allowing values between the two ends.
Applying **sigmoid** changes the activation rule while keeping the input and weights fixed. Each selected hidden neuron transforms its weighted sum into a value between zero and one.
children: The **320 and 2,000** inputs remain formants in hertz. **Purple** identifies hidden neurons still using their linear value; **green** identifies ones with sigmoid applied after their weighted sum.

teaching.text: A changed activation becomes a changed input to the next layer. **All later activations must therefore be recalculated**, using the updated values rather than the old linear results.
children: **Hidden layer 3, neuron 4** locates one neuron in the network. In **σ(−0.076) = 0.481**, −0.076 is its updated weighted sum and 0.481 is the value passed on after sigmoid. The layer and neuron numbers locate the operation; the decimals are its input and output values.

teaching.text: Applying sigmoid across the hidden neurons changes the preferred vowel. The final **32% for Dan** is the largest output probability, so the choice still differs from the dean target.
children: The output percentages come from **softmax** over the vowel alternatives, separate from the individual hidden sigmoid activations.
This is an **activation-function effect**, rather than learning: the processing rule changed while the weights stayed fixed.

teaching.text: The program places **nn.Sigmoid** after each hidden **nn.Linear**. Linear calculates a weighted sum, and Sigmoid transforms that result before the next layer receives it.
children: **X** is the formant-input table, **Y** is the correct-vowel table, and **net** is the network processing X. **Linear(2, 3)** takes two inputs and produces three weighted-sum values.
**nn.Sigmoid()** changes those values while keeping their count at three. The layer widths therefore remain **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**.

teaching.text: The hidden sigmoid and the final softmax have different jobs.
children: **Sigmoid** transforms each hidden neuron’s value separately into a value between zero and one.

**Softmax** treats the five final scores together to form probabilities that add up to one. The final Linear layer supplies scores to the cross-entropy loss, which handles the probability-related calculation.

teaching.text: Other activation functions, including **ReLU**, can be tested in place of sigmoid to examine how the choice affects vowel recognition.

In this **fully connected neural network**, every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer. Its input **F1 and F2** measurements are frequencies of the first two vocal-tract resonances, in **Hz**, or cycles per second.
children: Input neurons receive those two measurements from one recording. Hidden layers process them. The five output neurons represent the vowels in done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.

teaching.text: Each connection has a **weight** that controls how the incoming value contributes to a weighted sum. The weights hold the learned information used for recognition.
children: The sequence **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** counts neurons in successive layers. Those counts differ from the changing **activation**, or response value, inside a neuron.
Random initial weights have not yet learned the vowel patterns. Training compares the network’s answer with a known target and changes the weights to reduce the mismatch.

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** sends the input through the processing layers. Each neuron calculates an **inner product**, multiplying incoming values by their weights and adding the products.
children: The example supplies **F1 = 320 Hz** and **F2 = 2,000 Hz**. In **w₁F1 + w₂F2**, **w₁** and **w₂** name the two connection weights into the top hidden neuron.
A number **inside a hidden circle** is its activation. A number **on a connecting line** is a weight. **−0.4 appears in both places** here, so its position determines which role it has.
For that neuron, the F1 contribution is positive and the F2 contribution is negative. Their combined effect gives the negative activation passed to the next layer.

teaching.text: **Softmax** converts the final **scores**, or **logits zᵢ**, into **probabilities pᵢ** over the five vowels. The probabilities total one, and a larger score gives a larger probability.
children: The index **i** identifies a vowel alternative, and **Σ** in the softmax expression means to add across those alternatives.
**55.7% for done** is the highest probability, so done is the network’s choice. The percentage reports confidence in a vowel category, rather than a frequency in hertz.
Here the network selects done, although the low F1 and high F2 belong to /i/, as in dean. The prediction and the known answer therefore differ.

teaching.text: The vowel plot places **F1 on the horizontal axis** and **F2 on the vertical axis**, both in **Hz**. Each point is one recording, and its color identifies the known vowel.
children: **525 observations** counts all the plotted recordings, with **105 tokens**, or recorded examples, for each vowel. The legend uses red for dean, magenta for Dan, blue for dune, cyan for Don and green for schwa in done.
Moving right means **higher F1**, and moving up means **higher F2**.

teaching.text: Each category forms a **cloud of points** because speakers and recordings vary. Dean tends toward low F1 and high F2, while Dan extends toward higher F1.
The clouds **overlap**, especially among dune, Don and done. A pair of formants in an overlapping region can fit more than one vowel category.
children: Training can improve recognition, but F1 and F2 do not always provide enough information to separate the vowels perfectly. Some measurement errors also remain in the data.

teaching.text: The **Computed Output** percentages give the current prediction. The **Desired Output**, or **target**, specifies the vowel that actually produced the formants.
children: A **one-hot target** has a one for the correct vowel and zeros for the others. Here the one beside **dean** identifies the answer for this recording.

teaching.text: The **loss** measures the mismatch between those outputs. Learning should make dean more likely and the incorrect alternatives less likely.

**Backpropagation** calculates how the loss depends on the weights, working from the output back toward the input. **SGD**, or stochastic gradient descent, uses that calculation to adjust the weights in small steps.
children: In the weight-update expression, **W** is a weight, **L** is the loss, and **η** is the learning rate. The **gradient**, written **∂L/∂W**, describes how changing that weight affects the loss. The left arrow means to replace the current weight with its adjusted value.

The connection numbers show weights being adjusted. The values inside the circles are saved **forward-pass activations**, reused for the backward calculation. A new forward pass recalculates them using the changed weights, which can improve the prediction.

teaching.text: The **circled +0.1 weight** multiplies the positive **1.57 activation** feeding done. Increasing that weight increases its contribution to done’s output score and probability.
children: Because dean is the target, raising done’s probability makes the error worse. Decreasing this marked weight is the useful direction.

teaching.text: The **circled +0.005** is an early connection weight from F1. Changing it changes a hidden activation, then later activations, before the output probabilities change.
children: Its small numerical size does not reveal the useful adjustment direction. Its effect passes through later positive and negative weights, so the backward calculation must account for the whole path to the error.

teaching.text: The last weights have the **most direct effect on the output error**. Early weights affect that error through the layers between them and the output.
children: **W2** names the first set of processing weights, and **W5** names the last set. The subscripts identify their positions in this network; each set contains many individual connection weights.

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming** reuses the results of smaller dependent calculations. In backpropagation, calculating the output-side error first provides the information needed to calculate the influence of earlier weights.
children: The earlier-weight calculation includes the later-weight effects, so the backward order avoids solving those later effects again from scratch.

teaching.text: The two learning ideas play different roles. **SGD** makes gradual weight adjustments; **dynamic programming** organizes the backward calculation that determines those adjustments.
Training pairs each recording with its known answer in two **matrices**, or tables of numbers.
children: **Formant_Inputs, 110 × 2** means 110 recording rows with the two columns **F1 and F2**. **TrueVowel_Outputs, 110 × 5** means matching rows with five vowel-answer columns.

In the highlighted row, **320 and 2,000 Hz** are the formants for one dean recording. Its **one-hot target** has one in the dean column and zeros in the other columns, so the five entries describe one answer.
The matching rows must **stay aligned** across the two tables.

teaching.text: Learning compares the computed output with the target and changes the weights. The target remains fixed, because it records the vowel that was actually produced.
children: A confident correct output leaves little error to correct. However, a correct choice on some examples does not by itself establish that the network has learned the general pattern.

teaching.text: The PyTorch **import** commands provide the neural-network tools.
children: **X** holds the formant-input table and **Y** holds the target table. Their shown sizes, **110 × 2** and **110 × 5**, count recording rows and measurement or answer columns. **torch.load** reads the saved tables, and **float** puts their entries in a numerical format that supports decimal values.

teaching.text: **Sequential** orders the layers. Each **Linear** instruction specifies a processing layer that takes weighted sums of its inputs.
children: **net** is the network variable. **net(X)** means process the input table X through that network. In **Linear(2, 3)**, two values enter and three neuron values come out.
The sizes **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** carry two formants through the hidden layers to five vowel scores. The input neurons receive values without a separate processing instruction.

teaching.text: **SGD** supplies the weight-update method. The variable **sgd** holds the procedure that applies it.
children: The update procedure **sgd** receives the trainable weights from **net.parameters()**. **lr = 0.1** sets the learning rate, controlling the size of each adjustment.

**zero_grad()** clears the previous stored weight-change information. The **CrossEntropyLoss** call compares **net(X)**, the computed scores, with **Y**, the known answers, and **loss** stores the mismatch.
**loss.backward()** calculates how that loss depends on the weights. **sgd.step()** applies the weight adjustment.
A larger step can move learning faster but can be less precise. A smaller step moves more slowly.

teaching.text: This code uses **all rows in one update**. The saved tables supply the examples; the learning commands supply the comparison and the weight change.
The S-shaped **sigmoid**, written **σ**, is an activation function that turns a weighted sum **z** into a value between zero and one.
children: The horizontal **Linear Activation** axis plots z, and the vertical **Sigmoid Activation** axis plots σ(z). The marked **(−4, 0.018)** and **(4, 0.982)** points give an input sum followed by its response.
Strongly negative inputs approach zero, and strongly positive inputs approach one. These are neuron responses, separate from probabilities over the five vowels.

teaching.text: The middle of the curve is steep, so small input changes can cause substantial output changes. The ends are flatter, so even larger input changes have little effect there.
The near **on-or-off** behavior associated with biological neurons motivates this bounded activation. The artificial sigmoid still allows intermediate values rather than only exact zero or exact one.
Applying **sigmoid** to a hidden neuron changes the value it passes on, while the input formants and weights stay fixed.
children: The **320 and 2,000** inputs remain formants in hertz. **Purple** identifies hidden neurons still using their linear value; **green** identifies ones with sigmoid applied after their weighted sum.

teaching.text: Every later layer must use that updated value. **Recalculate the downstream weighted sums and activations** after each switch, because their inputs have changed.
children: **Hidden layer 3, neuron 4** locates one neuron in the network. In **σ(−0.076) = 0.481**, −0.076 is its updated weighted sum and 0.481 is the value passed on after sigmoid. The layer and neuron numbers locate the operation; the decimals are its input and output values.

teaching.text: Applying sigmoid across the hidden neurons changes the preferred vowel. The final **32% for Dan** is the largest output probability, so the choice still differs from the dean target.
children: The output percentages come from **softmax** over the vowel alternatives, separate from the individual hidden sigmoid activations.
This is an **activation-function effect**, rather than learning: the processing rule changed while the weights stayed fixed.

teaching.text: The program places **nn.Sigmoid** after each hidden **nn.Linear**. Linear calculates a weighted sum, and Sigmoid transforms that result before the next layer receives it.
children: **X** is the formant-input table, **Y** is the correct-vowel table, and **net** is the network processing X. **Linear(2, 3)** takes two inputs and produces three weighted-sum values.
**nn.Sigmoid()** changes those values while keeping their count at three. The layer widths therefore remain **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**.

teaching.text: The final Linear layer supplies five scores to **CrossEntropyLoss**. The loss compares those scores with the targets and handles the softmax-related calculation.
children: The hidden sigmoid transforms each neuron separately. The final probability calculation compares the vowel alternatives together.

teaching.text: **Initialization** is the choice of starting weights. This run starts with one random initialization and repeatedly updates the same linear network on the vowel data.
children: **Seed 0** identifies this run’s random starting point. The code’s **X = Formant_Inputs / 1000** changes frequency units from hertz to kilohertz; it keeps the same recordings and their relative formant values.

teaching.text: The graph shows **training accuracy**, the percentage of training examples whose highest-scoring output matches the correct vowel. It measures performance on the training recordings, rather than a separate set of new recordings.
children: The horizontal **Epoch** axis counts training passes. Here each pass uses all **525 training recordings** for one weight update, repeated **2,000** times at learning rate **0.1**. The vertical axis gives percent correct on those same recordings.

**model** is the linear network, **loss_fn** measures error, and **opt** applies SGD updates. The target variable **y** is extracted by **argmax**, which selects the vowel column containing the target’s largest value.
With **five vowel alternatives**, chance performance is about **20%**, or one correct guess in five. Knowing nothing therefore does not mean getting every answer wrong.

teaching.text: Accuracy rises and then levels off at **44.95%** in this displayed run. A flat part is a **plateau**, where more updates produce little visible improvement.
children: For measuring accuracy, **pred** selects the highest-scoring category for each recording, **correct** is the fraction matching y, and **accuracy** stores the percentages for plotting.

teaching.text: These runs keep the **data and network structure the same** and change the **random starting weights**. Each curve follows one initialization through learning.
children: The legend’s **Seed 0–Seed 9** labels identify ten random initializations. Each seed starts a fresh model and optimizer; it is not a vowel category or an additional input measurement.

teaching.text: The curves take different paths: some improve earlier, while others stay near a plateau longer. All the displayed runs finish at **44.95% training accuracy**.
children: The horizontal **Epoch** axis counts full-data training passes, and the vertical axis gives **training accuracy in percent**. Every run uses the same 525 recordings, layer widths, learning rate and update count.
After converging, the curves overlap, so several runs can lie along the same visible line. Different starting weights can affect the learning path even when the final accuracy is the same.

teaching.text: The plateau stays below perfect accuracy. **Overlap among the vowel formants** helps explain why using only F1 and F2 makes perfect separation difficult.
A **vector** is a list of numbers. This vowel network takes one **static vector** of two measurements, **F1 and F2**, and returns five vowel-category scores.
children: An input entry describes the recording; an output entry describes one possible answer. **Static** means one fixed list from one moment.

teaching.text: In **parallel distributed processing**, neurons within a layer calculate responses in parallel, and information is spread across many neurons.
children: The weights determine how the numbers are processed. Backpropagation supports learning by relating errors to those weights.
The early **McCulloch and Pitts** model used the all-or-none character of neural activity. The **Parallel Distributed Processing** books developed the network approach.

teaching.text: Speech and language also involve **sequences**. Formants change over time, and words arrive in an order. Modeling those patterns requires using information across moments, rather than only one fixed input vector.

A **recurrent neural network** uses **feedback**: output from one moment returns through state units and affects processing at the next moment. This allows the current response to depend on recent history.
In **Jordan’s network**, plan units specify the sequence to produce, hidden units combine information, output units produce the response, and state units carry information from recent outputs.
children: The arrows from **output units back to state units** carry the recent output into another processing moment. The small loops at the state units show that retained state also contributes to its update.
Both the plan and the retained state feed the hidden layer to influence the next response.

teaching.text: The speech-production traces show that articulatory features can extend across several sounds. Rounding, for example, can rise early and stay active through part of the sequence.
children: The traces are labeled **Voice, Place, Sonorant, Sibilant, Nasal, Height, Back and Round**. Each follows one speech-feature response across the horizontal **Time** steps, numbered 0 to 32. A rising trace means a stronger feature response, not a higher acoustic frequency.

teaching.text: A **single neuron** takes an input vector and returns one weighted sum. A **neural network** connects many neurons so that one input vector produces an output vector, such as scores for five vowels.
children: In the single-neuron diagram, **x** is the input vector, each **w** is a connection weight, **Σ** means add the weighted inputs, and **y** is the one resulting response. Seven input circles illustrate seven values entering one neuron.
In the network diagram, **W1, W2 and W3** label sets of weights between processing stages. The five output circles form a decision vector, with one value per alternative.

teaching.text: A **large language model**, or **LLM**, takes a sequence of vectors and predicts the next item. Each vector is a list of numbers representing an item such as a word.
children: **Vectors 1–15 in** counts fifteen context items; **16** marks the next item to predict. The bars labeled **PDF** give its probability distribution over alternatives.
The **context window** is the sequence available for prediction. Fifteen vectors illustrate the idea, rather than set a fixed limit on context length.
Layers of learned weights transform the input representations until the model produces probabilities for the next item.

teaching.text: For **learning**, an existing sequence supplies the correct continuation. Predicting the next word and comparing that prediction with the real word gives an error for backpropagation and **SGD** to use.
An **agentic system** connects whole LLMs with different jobs. One produces an outline, another writes a draft, a critic checks it, and a reviser changes it.
children: The arrows between the **Outline, Write, Critic, Revise and Final LLM** boxes carry messages between whole models. The return arrow from reviser to critic is the feedback loop used to check a revised draft again.
**Hallucination** means producing invented information. Criticism and revision aim to detect and reduce it before the final answer is produced.

teaching.text: **Inference** uses learned weights to produce an answer. **Learning** changes those weights through error-based adjustments.
children: In **SGD + DP**, SGD is stochastic gradient descent and **DP** is dynamic programming. The label combines gradual weight adjustments with the backward organization of the error calculation.

teaching.text: **Gestalt completion** uses the structure already present to supply missing information. The next-item task trains a system to supply a missing continuation from the available sequence.
A model can use known sequence items **x₁ through x₁₅** to predict **x₁₆**. The vectors can represent several kinds of material.
children: The subscript locates an item in the sequence. Each **vector column** contains several numerical entries describing that one item.

teaching.text: For **words**, the sentence so far supplies the context. In “The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the …”, predicting a continuation requires tracking that the cat is the one that sat.
For **sound**, consecutive spectrogram frames become vectors, with the illustrated **0–5 kHz** scale identifying the frequencies represented in each frame.
children: For **images**, the image is divided into **sixteen ordered patches**, read row by row. Fifteen known patches supply the context for predicting the missing sixteenth.

teaching.text: For a **protein**, the sequence consists of amino acids. The insulin example leaves the next amino acid to be predicted.
children: The letters **F, V, N** and the other letters on the protein chain are **amino-acid codes**. They identify the sequence items; they are not the neural network’s weights or formant names.
Words, sound frames, image patches and amino acids reach the model as lists of numbers. The material differs, but the next-item task remains the same.

teaching.text: **Phonotactic knowledge** is knowledge of the sound sequences a language allows. English permits a simple **C V C** syllable, where C means **consonant sound** and V means **vowel sound**, as in mat, cup and dog.
children: The colored vowels identify that position in the written examples.
The pattern concerns sounds. Two letters can spell one consonant sound, as in ship, and a silent letter does not add a sound.

teaching.text: An **onset** is the consonant or consonant group before a syllable’s vowel. A **coda** is the consonant or consonant group after it.
children: English allows some consonant orders and excludes others. Flat is possible, but the starred lfat is not. Help is possible, but hepl is not. A star marks an impossible English form.

teaching.text: A longer word contains several syllables. In **At·lan·tic**, the middle dots mark syllable boundaries: t and l can meet across a boundary, although tl cannot begin an English syllable.
children: The **star** in ***tlantic** marks an excluded English syllable pattern.
The ng sound can end a syllable, as in ring, but it cannot begin one in English.

teaching.text: **Next-letter prediction** reveals knowledge of possible English sequences. Some beginnings allow many continuations, while others sharply restrict the next letter.
children: The **underscore** is the next-letter position to fill. The **green letters** are possible continuations, while a **starred sequence** marks an excluded beginning such as ***spn**.

teaching.text: After **ra**, many letters are possible because the vowel has already arrived. After **skr**, a vowel is expected. After **sp**, l, r or a vowel can follow, while n is excluded in this onset pattern.
children: The predictions follow spelling as well as sound. After k, n is possible in a word such as knee, even though the k is silent.

teaching.text: A **probability distribution** can express these expectations. Many plausible continuations produce a broad distribution; strong constraints concentrate probability on a few choices.
children: The **x₁₆** label identifies the next-item prediction in the sequence model. These short word beginnings use the same idea with fewer preceding letters; it does not mean every example already contains fifteen letters.
Learning to predict the next letter requires learning the sound and spelling patterns that make those predictions accurate.

teaching.text: A **neuron** receives an input vector **x** and calculates one weighted sum. The connection **w** values weight its inputs, **Σ** means add those contributions, and **y** is its one response.
children: A **neural network** combines many neurons and returns a decision vector, with one score for each possible answer.

teaching.text: A **large language model** processes a sequence of vectors to predict the next item. Its layers change the numerical representation of the sequence, ending in a distribution over possible continuations.
children: **Vectors 1–15** count the illustrated context items; **16** marks the item being predicted. **PDF** labels the probability distribution over that item’s possible values. The **W** labels identify learned weight sets, not input items.

teaching.text: An **agentic system** connects whole language models with different jobs. The **Outline, Write, Critic, Revise and Final LLM** boxes represent those roles, and their arrows carry messages between models.
children: The return arrow from reviser to critic forms a loop for checking the changed draft again.
The models communicate through messages in human or computer languages.

teaching.text: **Inference** produces an answer using learned weights. **Learning** compares predictions with targets and adjusts those weights.
children: In **SGD + DP**, **SGD** means stochastic gradient descent, supplying gradual weight adjustments. **DP** means dynamic programming, organizing the backward error calculation that determines them.

teaching.text: A **representation** is the information about an item carried in its vector. An LLM changes these representations through many layers to make a useful next-item prediction.
children: The columns labeled **vectors 1–15 in** represent fifteen input items. Each column is a vector of numbers, and **x** names the item representation being transformed.

teaching.text: Several **heads** work in parallel within a layer. The horizontal **heads** arrow follows these contributions, and the colored **W** blocks represent their learned weights.
children: The layer combines the heads’ contributions into updated representations.

teaching.text: Successive layers use the representations produced by the layer before them. The result of one stage becomes the input for another, allowing the information to develop through the model.
children: The **five-layer vertical stack** counts those successive processing stages, rather than words in the context. **16 PDF** marks the probability distribution for the next item after the fifteen inputs.

teaching.text: A **dynamical system** applies a rule to its current state to produce a new state, then uses that updated state again. Its **trajectory** is the sequence of states that results.
children: For the oscillator, **x** is position and **v** is velocity. The subscripts **n** and **n+1** mark the current and next update, and **h** is the step size between updates. The equations update position using velocity, then update velocity using the new position.
**x₀ and x₁**, and **v₀ and v₁**, locate successive state values in the two plots. The horizontal **n →** axis follows the update steps of the back-and-forth trajectory.

teaching.text: A **recurrent network** carries its recent output back through state units as processing continues over time. The same learned connections are used at each time step.
children: The **copy** arrow sends output values back to the **state** units. Those stored values join the **plan** inputs to influence the hidden units at the next time step.

teaching.text: In an **LLM**, the vectors change as they pass through successive layers. Depth supplies the sequence of changes: each layer uses the values produced by the preceding layer.
children: **W₁ through W₅** name the layers’ separate weight sets. The colored paths at the right follow representation values through depth; those values do not have to follow an oscillator’s repeating curve.

teaching.text: The stock-return paths show different values developing along different trajectories. A trajectory describes how a quantity changes across the ordered stages being followed.
A **vector** is a list of numbers, so different kinds of material can be represented in the same general form. The model uses an ordered sequence of vectors to predict the next item.
children: **x₁ through x₁₅** name the fifteen context items; **x₁₆** is the next prediction. The values inside each vector represent one item, while the subscripts locate items in the sequence.

teaching.text: For **words**, the preceding sentence supplies the context. In “The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the …”, the continuation depends on the sentence structure, including which animal sat.
For **sound**, consecutive spectrogram frames become vectors. They follow time, with frequency recorded on the vertical spectrogram axis.
children: For **images**, the grid has **fifteen known patches and a missing sixteenth patch**, read in row-by-row order.

teaching.text: For a **protein**, the letters on the chain are **amino-acid codes**. The next amino acid in this insulin sequence is **Y**.
children: Here **Y** names an amino acid, while the lower-case y in the separate neuron diagram names its output value.
The original materials differ, but each task uses the preceding vector representations to predict the following one.

teaching.text: **Phonotactic knowledge** tells which sound sequences English allows. A simple **C V C** syllable has a **consonant sound, vowel sound and consonant sound**, as in mat, cup and dog.
children: The pattern counts sounds rather than letters. The sh in ship spells one consonant sound, and a silent final e does not add a sound.

teaching.text: The **onset** comes before the vowel, and the **coda** comes after it. English allows particular consonant orders in each position.
children: Flat and help are possible words, while the starred lfat and hepl violate the allowed order. The l is next to the vowel in both of the allowed examples.

teaching.text: **Syllable boundaries** also matter. The dots in **At·lan·tic** locate the boundaries: t and l can meet across one, but tl cannot begin an English syllable.
children: A **star**, as in ***tlantic**, marks an excluded English pattern.
The ng sound can occur at the end of a syllable, as in ring, but cannot start one in English.

teaching.text: Predicting the **next letter** depends on the sequence already present. Some beginnings allow many completions, while others permit only a few.
children: The **underscore** is the next-letter position. Green letters give possible continuations, and the **star** marks excluded sequences such as ***spn**.

teaching.text: After **ra**, several consonants can follow. After **skr**, the next letter is a vowel. After **sp**, l, r or a vowel can follow, while n is excluded from that onset pattern.
children: Spelling also matters. After k, n can occur in knee, although that k does not represent a spoken sound.

teaching.text: The prediction can be expressed as a **probability distribution** over letters. A broad distribution allows many continuations; a concentrated one gives most of its probability to the few continuations that fit.
children: **x₁₆** names the next-item prediction in the sequence model. In these shorter word beginnings, the blank is simply the item after the available letters; fifteen preceding letters are not required.
The model can improve only by learning regularities in the words it is trying to continue. Accurate next-letter prediction therefore reveals knowledge of English sound and spelling patterns.

teaching.text: A **character-level transformer** is an LLM trained to predict the next character, or letter. Existing words supply both the sequence so far and the correct next letter.
children: Training compares the prediction with the true continuation and adjusts the weights. Better predictions require learning which sound and spelling sequences English permits.

teaching.text: The small model has **four heads in each of five layers**. The heads count parallel processing components within a layer; the layers count successive stages of representation changes.
children: A **token** is an input item represented by a vector. **64-dimensional** means its vector has 64 numerical entries, rather than 64 separate tokens.

teaching.text: Generated word examples reveal the model’s current knowledge. Early outputs can be poorly formed; more training and more words can help the output reflect English syllable patterns.

review.scope: All70sourcepages in Lectures14–18 reviewed against C2, sourceText, speakerNotes, original previews and supplied transcript evidence. Only new V3 teaching replacements are supplied; unmapped pages inherit C2. No previous edition or UI file is changed.
review.staticReview: All70previews inspected in collection contact sheets, with32targeted full-size diagram/code/plot previews inspected for exact identifiers, axes, legends, numerical roles and repeated-number ambiguities.
review.mediaReview: Three sampled frames at8%,45%and82%of each of8unique original L14videos inspected. Frame sampling supports the visible labels, positions and representative states; it is not full animation/audio inspection. Existing source transcript and inventories supply movement explanations.
review.knownSourceIssue: L14p23 subtitle calls negative weights orange, while the visible negative labels are green. V3 explains the signed values and actual connection positions without teaching that inconsistent color rule.
review.teachingStyle: Identifiers are defined inside their conceptual explanation; no detached glossary, repeated labels, fixed bullet count, outside theory, class narration, or worked arithmetic.
review.trainingCurveProvenance: The L16p15–16 source figures show executed NumPy reference runs alongside requested PyTorch code. This construction distinction is retained here rather than inserted into spoken teaching. Teaching retains the actual graph conditions:525trainingexamples,full-batchupdates,randominitializations,seeds0–9,2,000updates,learningrate0.1and44.95%finaltrainingaccuracy.
review.terminologyPreference: Name the system, motion, mode or pattern directly. Use model or distribution where appropriate, and image/image patch for literal visual inputs. Avoid picture as a substitute for the subject.
